title: Thirty-nine kinds of work
hook: Shabbat's labors are drawn from building the tabernacle (Mishnah Shabbat 7:2)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moed, the second order of the Mishnah, the book of appointed times. Your line was holy time has rules. Did you look at the month ahead? A new week starts today. Day one thousand seventy-two.

Read the list out loud and something odd happens. Sowing. Plowing. Reaping. Binding sheaves. Threshing. Winnowing. Selecting. Grinding. Sifting. Kneading. Baking. By the time you reach the end, there's bread on the table. Keep going and a sheep turns into a garment: shearing, washing, combing, dyeing, spinning, weaving, sewing. Then an animal hide becomes a surface you can write two letters on. The list is a law, from the Mishnah's tractate on Shabbat. But it reads like a walk through a village from dawn to dusk. Today: why a law about rest is built like a story about making things.
screen: `FIELD TO BREAD.` → `SHEEP TO GARMENT.` → `HIDE TO TWO LETTERS.`

segments.voice: Avot melacha. Avot means fathers, so these are the fathers of work, the main categories. The Mishnah opens its list by giving the total: forty less one. Back in year one you met the big idea, that the rabbis connect these kinds of work to the building of the tabernacle. Today, look at the machinery. First, the order. The list doesn't jump around. It follows whole chains of making: bread, then cloth, then the hide for writing, then building and tearing down, putting out and kindling a fire, the final hammer blow that finishes a thing, and carrying from one domain to another. The Talmud notices this. It asks why baking is on the list when the tabernacle needed dyes cooked, not bread baked, and answers that the Mishnah followed the order of bread. The list was built to be remembered, chain by chain. Second, the family. If there are fathers, there are offspring. The rabbis call them toldot, the descendants: acts that share the father's purpose without looking like it. The Talmud gives one: pruning a tree counts under planting, because both help a plant grow. So the thirty-nine aren't a fence around thirty-nine actions. They are thirty-nine questions you can ask of any new act: which father does this belong to? Third, why count at all? The Mishnah's own setting is a case of someone who forgot. In its rulings, how many fathers you broke matters for what you owe. A definition, not a mood. That's the point of today's line. Shabbat doesn't say rest however you like. It says here is what work is, defined, so that what's left over can be rest.
screen: `AVOT: THE FATHERS OF WORK.` · `CHAINS OF MAKING: BREAD, CLOTH, SCROLL.` · `TOLDOT: THE OFFSPRING.` · `COUNTED, SO IT'S DEFINED.` · then, large: `WORK, DEFINED.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: notice one kind of work you do. Sit, and let your breath slow. Pick something you did yesterday with your hands or your screen. Cooking, typing, fixing, sorting, carrying. Now play the rabbis' game with it. Trace it back. What is it really doing? Making something new? Changing a thing from one state to another? Moving it from one place to another? Find its father. You don't have to stop doing it. Just see it clearly, as a kind of making. The bell holds the time.
Avot melacha. The fathers of work: the main categories set aside on Shabbat, with their offspring, the toldot, growing out of them. Today's word.
Your line: work, defined. Today, when you start a task, name its father in your head: planting, building, writing, carrying. Day one thousand seventy-two.

howItsDone: Jews who keep Shabbat according to halacha study the categories of work and their derivatives, and rabbis apply them to new situations; other Jews keep Shabbat through rest, meals and synagogue in their own ways.
